headline: P0014 (Family Practice, GA): 99215 share of 34.4% against 16.7% expected; the excess sits mostly with very complex patients, not low-complexity ones
rationale: This panel is heavily complex: 1,669 of 2,500 visits are for patients with 5+ chronic conditions. That explains part of the 34.4% 99215 share, but the share is still about double the 16.7% expected for this patient mix (z=4.44, risk-adjusted score 8.80). For low-complexity patients the provider's rates are close to peers: 0/8 for 0 conditions, 4/53 (7.5% vs 3.4%) for 1 condition on a small base, 5.1% vs 5.6% for 2 conditions and 9.1% vs 8.7% for 3. That means the concern the rules focus on, high-level billing on simple patients, is mostly absent. Sampled low-complexity 99215s do exist, including C0005487 (obesity only, E66.9) and C0005505/C0006995 (the same diabetic patient billed 99215 twice a week apart). The bigger gap is inside the high-complexity groups: 19.6% vs 13.9% at 4 conditions and 45.4% vs 29.8% at 5+. Some sampled high-complexity 99215s list only routine or narrow diagnoses for the visit, such as C0005582 (osteoarthritis plus URI, J06.9), C0007445 (I10 plus Z09 follow-up) and C0006841 (E78.5 only). Billing is also almost entirely 99214/99215, with just 5 claims at 99211/99212. Taken together, the pattern is consistent with either a genuinely high-acuity panel or level inflation within complex patients. The claim lists are random samples, and without clinical documentation (MDM complexity, time, problems addressed) the packet cannot tell these apart.
next_steps: Request and audit progress notes for a stratified sample of 99215s, especially in the 4 and 5+ condition groups, against 2021+ E/M MDM or time criteria.
Review the low-complexity 99215s (C0005178, C0005487, C0005505, C0006995), including why the same patient (P0014-N0048) had two 99215 visits seven days apart.

Check whether the diagnoses on high-complexity 99215 claims reflect the problems actually addressed at the visit (for example C0005582 with J06.9 and C0007445 with Z09), rather than a background list of chronic conditions.
Compare the provider's 99214/99215 distribution and almost unused 99211-99213 levels against Family Practice peers with similar case mix, and look at the trend over time.
Verify that chronic-condition counts come from independent claims history and are not driven by the provider's own coding.
